q: Why ask 'What does this require ME to do, by when, at what cost?' instead of 'summarise this'?
options: It produces a shorter summary
A summary lists everything; a decisions-relevant summary extracts only what matters for action
It stops the AI from making mistakes
Longer prompts are always better
explanation: A generic summary reports the document. A decisions-relevant summary converts it into actions, deadlines and costs — the only part a busy professional needs.

q: For a document too long to paste at once, the lesson says to:
options: Give up and read it fully
Paste it in sections, summarise each, then combine the summaries
Ask the AI to guess the missing parts
Only paste the last page
explanation: Paste section by section with the same four questions, then combine. The AI only knows what you paste — never let it guess the missing sections.

q: What does 'numbers without formulas' mean in practice?
options: AI does arithmetic in chat only, no spreadsheet
You describe the table and what to calculate; AI writes the spreadsheet formulas and explains them
You must memorise Excel formulas first
Spreadsheets cannot be built without paid software
explanation: You describe columns, rows and calculations in plain language; the AI produces the layout and formulas and explains each in one sentence. You type no formulas.

q: A document you must summarise is confidential. What does the lesson say?
options: Paste it — confidentiality does not matter for summaries
Summarise a public policy document for practice instead
Type the whole document from memory instead
Ask the AI to promise confidentiality
explanation: Confidential documents never go into free AI tools. Practise on a public document; the skill transfers unchanged.

q: After the AI builds your spreadsheet totals, you should:
options: Trust it — spreadsheets are always accurate
Add one row by hand and compare against the AI's total
Delete the formulas to be safe
Rebuild it from scratch in Excel
explanation: AI arithmetic is usually right and occasionally confidently wrong. One hand-checked row catches that — the Day 2 verification habit applied to numbers.
